screens.title: Migrating SQL Server Databases to Azure SQL
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn why and how organizations move existing S Q L Server databases to Azure S Q L Database or Azure S Q L Managed Instance. We begin with the decision drivers: compatibility needs, server-level features, and acceptable downtime. Then we show two practical migration patterns—offline exports using BACPAC files for simple, lower-risk moves, and online migrations using Azure Database Migration Service when you need minimal application downtime. You will also see how Azure Data Studio's S Q L Migration extension helps assess and orchestrate migrations and what common connectivity or permission pitfalls look like in practice. For example, we will walk through producing a BACPAC from a local S Q L Server, uploading it to Azure Blob Storage with a valid access token, and importing it into an Azure S Q L Database. We will also explain how DMS performs an initial full data load and then replicates changes for a short cutover window. Finally, we'll review essential post-migration tasks such as updating connection strings, reconfiguring logins, and reindexing. By the end, you'll know which migration pattern fits your scenario and how to avoid common failures like expired SAS tokens or blocked network paths.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Migrating SQL Server
Migrating SQL Server Databases to Azure SQL
Choose the right target, plan for downtime, and execute reliable offline or online migrations.
In this lesson

Understand the trade-offs between Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance, learn offline BACPAC flows, and plan online DMS migrations with connectivity and post-migration tasks.

Why it matters

Selecting the correct service and migration pattern reduces downtime, avoids compatibility surprises, and ensures applications remain available during cutover.

Explore Key Topics
BACPAC export, Azure Database Migration Service, Azure Data Studio extension.
BACPAC Offline
Simple export/import; requires downtime during export and import.
DMS Online
Continuous sync, minimal downtime, needs network connectivity.
Azure Data Studio
Guided assessments and DMS orchestration via the migration extension.
Interactive Concept
Target selection map
Azure SQL Database for modern apps; Managed Instance for lift-and-shift with server features like SQL Agent and cross-database queries.
Quick reference
BACPAC — schema and data package for offline import.
DMS — initial load then continuous sync for online migrations.
Azure Data Studio — guided wizard and assessment tooling.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to choose the appropriate Azure target for your S Q L Server workloads, execute a simple offline migration using a BACPAC file, and set up an online migration with Azure Database Migration Service for minimal downtime. You will also use Azure Data Studio's S Q L Migration extension to assess compatibility and orchestrate migration steps. Each skill matters because selecting the wrong target or tool can increase downtime, create compatibility regressions, or leave security gaps. For example, knowing when to use Managed Instance avoids rewriting server-level jobs and linked server logic. Understanding how to generate and validate a BACPAC ensures you can move small to medium databases reliably, and learning DMS configuration prevents cutover surprises by handling continuous synchronization. Finally, the ability to verify connectivity, storage access, and post-migration tasks means your application moves with minimal disruption and predictable behavior.

screens.title: Azure SQL Database vs Azure SQL Managed Instance
screens.narratorSegment: Start by framing the decision between the two main PaaS options. Azure S Q L Database is a fully managed database service optimized for modern cloud-native single-database or elastic pool scenarios. It removes server-level management responsibilities and is ideal when your application can be adapted to a database-level model. In contrast, Azure S Q L Managed Instance provides near 100 percent compatibility with on-premises S Q L Server, preserving server-level features such as S Q L Agent jobs, cross-database queries, and CLR. A concrete example: if your application uses S Q L Agent jobs to run scheduled maintenance or ETL tasks and uses cross-database joins, Managed Instance avoids rewriting those behaviors. A common misconception is that Azure S Q L Database and Managed Instance are interchangeable; they are not. Choosing the wrong target can force significant application changes or cause functional breaks. Key differences to check are feature compatibility, IP and network access needs, and acceptable refactor work. To decide, inventory server-level features used by your application, estimate refactor effort, and pick Managed Instance for lift-and-shift compatibility or Azure S Q L Database for cloud-native simplification. What server-level features does your app depend on today?

keyIdea.title: Decision rule
keyIdea.text: Use Managed Instance for high compatibility and server-level features; use Azure SQL Database for cloud-native single-database workloads.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Target comparison
Azure SQL Database
Managed, single-database model
  • Fully managed PaaS focused on single databases and elastic pools.
  • Best for cloud-native apps that can operate without server-level features.
  • Simplifies management but may require app refactoring for server features.
Example: A multi-tenant web app using one database per tenant benefits from Azure SQL Database scaling and reduced maintenance.
Azure SQL Managed Instance
Near 100% SQL Server compatibility
  • Supports server-level features: SQL Agent, cross-database queries, linked servers and CLR.
  • Ideal for lift-and-shift migrations where minimal code change is required.
  • Requires network configuration and subnet integration.
Example: An enterprise app relying on SQL Agent jobs and cross-database reporting should use Managed Instance to avoid rework.
Check
Inventory server-level features used today.
Tip
If server features are minimal, prefer Azure SQL Database for simpler ops.
Misconception
Assuming identical feature sets will cause migration pain.

screens.title: What is a BACPAC and when to use it
screens.narratorSegment: A BACPAC is a portable archive that contains both the schema and the data of a database. It is designed for offline migrations where a brief or planned downtime is acceptable. The typical workflow is to export a BACPAC from your source S Q L Server, upload the resulting file to Azure Blob Storage, then import it into an Azure S Q L Database. A concrete scenario: you have a reporting database that can be quiesced for maintenance windows; creating a BACPAC lets you move that database without complex replication. One common misconception is that BACPACs are suitable for very large, high-change production databases—because the export/import process requires quiescing the source or may take a long time, BACPAC is not ideal for systems that need continuous availability. Important operational notes: test the export locally first, ensure data integrity, and verify that your storage SAS token or account key grants read access to the Azure S Q L import process. Key takeaway: use BACPAC for straightforward, lower-volume moves where downtime is acceptable and schema/data fidelity matters. What is a BACPAC and when to use it means use bacpac for offline migrations that package schema and data into a portable file for import into azure sql database.. In practical terms, offline export/import for schema and data. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: BACPAC purpose
keyIdea.text: Use BACPAC for offline migrations that package schema and data into a portable file for import into Azure SQL Database.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › BACPAC
Definition
BACPAC file

A BACPAC is a compressed export of a database's schema and data. It is useful when the source can be taken offline or when a snapshot copy is acceptable.

Process
  1. Export BACPAC from source (SSMS or sqlpackage).
  2. Upload BACPAC to Azure Blob Storage and generate SAS.
  3. Import BACPAC into Azure SQL Database using portal, SSMS, or CLI.
When not to use
Avoid for large, highly transactional systems needing continuous availability or for migrations that require minimal downtime.
Example
Migrating a reporting database during a scheduled maintenance window using SSMS Export Data-tier Application and importing to Azure SQL Database.
Key Takeaway

BACPAC is simple and reliable for smaller or quiesced databases, but it requires downtime during export/import.

screens.title: Export and Import BACPAC — step-by-step
screens.narratorSegment: This lesson walks through the export and import steps to move a database using a BACPAC. Begin by exporting from S Q L Server Management Studio using the Export Data-tier Application wizard or sqlpackage. exe with an export action. Create a BACPAC file and validate it locally to ensure schema and data are present. Next, upload the file to Azure Blob Storage and create a Shared Access Signature token that grants read access and has an appropriate expiry. A common mistake is creating a SAS token with insufficient permissions or an incorrect expiry; always test the token by attempting to read the blob before starting the import. To import into Azure S Q L Database you can use the portal, SSMS import wizard, or the Azure CLI import command. Monitor the import operation and be prepared for the process to take time depending on size. After import, connect to the target database and validate row counts, indexes, and key application queries. Example command usage is shown in the code panel; read it as a conceptual call pattern and replace placeholders with your values during execution. The final takeaway: validate storage access and test the entire workflow in a non-production environment before a planned cutover.

keyIdea.text: Export with SSMS or sqlpackage, upload to Blob storage, generate a valid SAS, import with Azure CLI or portal, verify data and indexes.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › BACPAC Steps
Export steps
Create the BACPAC
  1. Use SSMS: Tasks → Export Data-tier Application and follow the wizard.
  2. Or use sqlpackage.exe /Action:Export to generate a .bacpac file.
  3. Validate the file locally before uploading.
Common mistake
Quiescing only partially or exporting while heavy DML is running can produce inconsistent snapshots.
Import via CLI
Azure CLI pattern
# Example import command (replace placeholders)
az sql db import \
  --resource-group <your-resource-group-name> \
  --server <your-azure-sql-server-name> \
  --name AdventureWorksLT_Migrated \
  --storage-key-type SharedAccessKey \
  --storage-key "<your-sas-token-for-blob>" \
  --storage-uri "https://<your-storage-account-name>.blob.core.windows.net/bacpac-files/AdventureWorksLT.bacpac" \
  --admin-user <azure-sql-server-admin-login> \
  --admin-password <azure-sql-server-admin-password> \
  --service-objective S0
Replace placeholders and run in Cloud Shell or a logged-in CLI. Monitor the operation until completion and validate the result in SSMS or Azure Data Studio.
Example check
Connect to the migrated database and compare row counts for key tables.
Pro tip
Test the full export/upload/import flow in a disposable environment to surface access issues early.
Key Takeaway

Ensure the SAS token and storage access work before starting the import to avoid failed imports and wasted time.

screens.title: Azure Database Migration Service (DMS) overview
screens.narratorSegment: Azure Database Migration Service is a managed service that enables online and offline migrations from on-premises S Q L Server to Azure targets. For online migrations, DMS performs an initial full data load and then continuously applies incremental changes so the target stays synchronized until you choose to cut over. The practical benefit is that your application can continue operating on the source during the bulk of migration and only needs a short maintenance window for cutover. A concrete example: for a transactional system that must remain available, DMS can synchronize changes using transaction log or change data capture mechanisms until point-in-time parity. A common misconception is that DMS eliminates planning; it does not. You must provision DMS in the correct region, ensure it has network access to the source (via VPN or ExpressRoute when needed), and select appropriate performance tiers. Typical steps are: provision DMS, create a migration project, configure source and target endpoints, select objects, start full load with continuous sync, monitor progress, validate the target, and perform cutover. Remember to test the entire flow and validate application behavior before fully switching to the target.

keyIdea.title: DMS claim
keyIdea.text: DMS enables continuous synchronization for online migrations, reducing downtime by applying incremental changes after an initial load.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Azure DMS
How it works
Initial load plus continuous sync
1. DMS performs a full data load to the target.
2. DMS applies incremental changes from transaction logs or CDC to keep the target synchronized.
3. When ready, you perform a cutover with minimal downtime.
Example: A retail checkout system remains online on source while DMS synchronizes sales transactions to the Managed Instance; cutover occurs during a brief window when traffic is low.
Requirements
  • Network connectivity from DMS to source (VPN/ExpressRoute or public endpoint and firewall rules).
  • Appropriate credentials and permissions for source and target endpoints.
  • Provisioning of a DMS instance in the correct subscription and region.
Misconception
DMS automates everything; you still must plan networking and validate migration scope.
Monitoring
Use DMS job monitoring to watch full load and continuous sync progress and to surface blocking errors.
Key Takeaway

DMS minimizes downtime via continuous synchronization, but it requires careful network and credential configuration.

screens.title: Provisioning DMS and performing cutover
screens.narratorSegment: Provisioning DMS and executing a safe cutover requires a sequence of deliberate steps. First, provision a DMS instance in the Azure portal in the same region and subscription as your target where possible. Next, create a migration project and specify the source type (S Q L Server) and the Azure target (S Q L Database or Managed Instance). Configure endpoints by providing connection strings and credentials for both source and target; validate these endpoints to confirm connectivity. Select the databases and tables to migrate and choose online migration to enable continuous synchronization. Start the migration: DMS performs the initial full load, then applies changes incrementally. Monitor the migration project until the change backlog is minimal and run validation tests against the target to ensure data fidelity. When ready, schedule a brief cutover: pause writes to the source or redirect traffic, complete final synchronization, validate application behavior against the new target, and then switch connections. A common mistake is performing cutover without exercising validation tests; always perform the cutover in a test window and have a rollback plan ready. After cutover, decommission DMS resources if they are no longer needed to avoid unexpected costs.

keyIdea.title: Cutover practice
keyIdea.text: Validate endpoints, monitor sync until backlog is minimal, run verification tests, then perform a brief, planned cutover with a rollback plan.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › DMS cutover
Provisioning and project setup
Create DMS instance and migration project
  1. Provision DMS in the portal and ensure region alignment.
  2. Create migration project: source SQL Server, target Azure SQL Database or Managed Instance.
  3. Configure and validate source/target endpoints and credentials.
Run and monitor
Full load, continuous sync, validate
  • Start migration: wait for initial full load to complete.
  • Monitor continuous sync until incremental backlog is minimal.
  • Run verification queries and application tests on the target.
Cutover checklist
Plan a short maintenance window, pause writes or switch traffic, finalize sync, validate behavior, update connection strings, and keep a rollback plan ready.
Key Takeaway

Monitoring and validation are essential; never cut over without testing the synchronized target under expected workloads.

Common mistake
Cutover without a validation run or rollback plan, leading to service disruption.

screens.title: Network and connectivity considerations
screens.narratorSegment: Network connectivity is often the dominant operational hurdle in migrations. Whether you use BACPAC imports or DMS, the migration tooling needs network access to the source and the target. For BACPAC imports the Azure S Q L import process must be able to read the blob where the BACPAC lives, so storage network rules and SAS token permissions must permit access. For DMS, the service needs to connect to your on-premises S Q L Server; this typically requires a VPN, ExpressRoute, or appropriately opened firewall ports. A concrete example: DMS cannot reach a database behind a corporate firewall unless the firewall allows traffic from the DMS service or a site-to-site link is configured. Common pitfalls include expired SAS tokens, restrictive storage firewall rules, and missing route configuration for subnets. Always validate connections before starting long-running migrations: test reading the blob with the SAS, run a simple connect test from a jump host to the source S Q L Server, and verify that the service principal or credentials used have required permissions. Finally, document and automate these checks so they are repeatable during future migrations. What network test would you run first in your environment to confirm DMS connectivity?

keyIdea.title: Network rule
keyIdea.text: Validate storage access and connectivity early. DMS requires network paths to the source, often via VPN or ExpressRoute; test and document them.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Connectivity
Key points
  • Ensure blob storage permits reads from the import process and that SAS tokens are valid.
  • For DMS, confirm a route to your on-premises SQL Server via VPN, ExpressRoute, or allowed public endpoints.
  • Open firewall ports and test credentials before starting migration jobs.
Validation checklist
- Test blob SAS read using a simple HTTP GET.
- Use a jump host to try connecting to the source SQL Server with the same credentials DMS will use.
- Verify storage network rules and DMS permissions.
Common failure
Expired SAS tokens or blocked storage/network rules causing import failures.
Pro tip
Automate connectivity tests and include them in migration runbooks to catch issues early.
Key Takeaway

Network and storage access problems are common—test them before exporting or starting DMS to avoid delays.

screens.title: Post-migration tasks and verification
screens.narratorSegment: A successful migration does not end at data copy; post-migration tasks ensure your application runs correctly and securely in Azure. Key activities include updating application connection strings to point to the new server or instance, creating or mapping logins and users so security principals match, re-indexing large tables, and updating statistics to help the query optimizer. You should run application integration tests and performance tests to confirm behavior under expected load. For example, after importing a BACPAC you may need to create server-level logins and map them to database users to restore access patterns. A common misconception is that data presence equals readiness; without reindexing or statistics updates, queries may perform poorly in the cloud. Also verify firewall rules, auditing, and backup configuration on the target. Keep a rollback plan and recent backups of the source in case you need to revert. screens.title: Common pitfalls and best practices
screens.narratorSegment: Common pitfalls often derail otherwise straightforward migrations. One frequent issue is storage access problems during BACPAC import: an incorrect SAS token, insufficient permissions, or restrictive storage firewall rules will cause the import to fail. Another is network misconfiguration for DMS: without a proper VPN, ExpressRoute, or opened firewall ports, DMS cannot reach on-premises sources. A third is insufficient validation after import or sync—skipping reindexing or missing login mappings can cause slow queries or broken authorization. Best practices to avoid these issues include: scripting and testing the full migration workflow in a non-production environment, validating SAS tokens and storage access before import, running connectivity checks for DMS endpoints, and preparing a post-migration checklist covering security, performance, and application tests. Also maintain a rollback plan with recent backups and keep stakeholders informed about the short cutover window required for final synchronization. Example mitigation: automate a connectivity test that attempts a sample S Q L connection and a blob read using the SAS token; if either fails, stop and resolve the issue before starting the full migration. These precautions prevent late surprises and make cutovers predictable.

In this lesson you will learn why and how organizations move existing S Q L Server databases to Azure S Q L Database or Azure S Q L Managed Instance. We begin with the decision drivers: compatibility needs, server-level features, and acceptable downtime. Then we show two practical migration patterns—offline exports using BACPAC files for simple, lower-risk moves, and online migrations using Azure Database Migration Service when you need minimal application downtime. You will also see how Azure Data Studio's S Q L Migration extension helps assess and orchestrate migrations and what common connectivity or permission pitfalls look like in practice. For example, we will walk through producing a BACPAC from a local S Q L Server, uploading it to Azure Blob Storage with a valid access token, and importing it into an Azure S Q L Database. We will also explain how DMS performs an initial full data load and then replicates changes for a short cutover window. Finally, we'll review essential post-migration tasks such as updating connection strings, reconfiguring logins, and reindexing. By the end, you'll know which migration pattern fits your scenario and how to avoid common failures like expired SAS tokens or blocked network paths.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to choose the appropriate Azure target for your S Q L Server workloads, execute a simple offline migration using a BACPAC file, and set up an online migration with Azure Database Migration Service for minimal downtime. You will also use Azure Data Studio's S Q L Migration extension to assess compatibility and orchestrate migration steps. Each skill matters because selecting the wrong target or tool can increase downtime, create compatibility regressions, or leave security gaps. For example, knowing when to use Managed Instance avoids rewriting server-level jobs and linked server logic. Understanding how to generate and validate a BACPAC ensures you can move small to medium databases reliably, and learning DMS configuration prevents cutover surprises by handling continuous synchronization. Finally, the ability to verify connectivity, storage access, and post-migration tasks means your application moves with minimal disruption and predictable behavior.

This second objectives slide focuses on operational skills and common troubleshooting checks you will practice. You will learn to validate storage access and SAS tokens when importing BACPAC files, to verify network connectivity for DMS including VPN or ExpressRoute considerations, and to implement post-migration activities like updating application connection strings and reindexing. These checks matter because many migrations fail or stall due to permission or network misconfiguration rather than data issues. For example, an expired SAS token blocks BACPAC imports; knowing how to generate and test a token prevents needless delays. You will also practice verifying user logins and role mappings after migration so your application maintains security and functionality. Together these outcomes make migrations repeatable and auditable. Start by framing the decision between the two main PaaS options. Azure S Q L Database is a fully managed database service optimized for modern cloud-native single-database or elastic pool scenarios. It removes server-level management responsibilities and is ideal when your application can be adapted to a database-level model. In contrast, Azure S Q L Managed Instance provides near 100 percent compatibility with on-premises S Q L Server, preserving server-level features such as S Q L Agent jobs, cross-database queries, and CLR. A concrete example: if your application uses S Q L Agent jobs to run scheduled maintenance or ETL tasks and uses cross-database joins, Managed Instance avoids rewriting those behaviors. A common misconception is that Azure S Q L Database and Managed Instance are interchangeable; they are not. Choosing the wrong target can force significant application changes or cause functional breaks. Key differences to check are feature compatibility, IP and network access needs, and acceptable refactor work. To decide, inventory server-level features used by your application, estimate refactor effort, and pick Managed Instance for lift-and-shift compatibility or Azure S Q L Database for cloud-native simplification. A BACPAC is a portable archive that contains both the schema and the data of a database. It is designed for offline migrations where a brief or planned downtime is acceptable. The typical workflow is to export a BACPAC from your source S Q L Server, upload the resulting file to Azure Blob Storage, then import it into an Azure S Q L Database. A concrete scenario: you have a reporting database that can be quiesced for maintenance windows; creating a BACPAC lets you move that database without complex replication. One common misconception is that BACPACs are suitable for very large, high-change production databases—because the export/import process requires quiescing the source or may take a long time, BACPAC is not ideal for systems that need continuous availability. Important operational notes: test the export locally first, ensure data integrity, and verify that your storage SAS token or account key grants read access to the Azure S Q L import process. Key takeaway: use BACPAC for straightforward, lower-volume moves where downtime is acceptable and schema/data fidelity matters. This lesson walks through the export and import steps to move a database using a BACPAC. Begin by exporting from S Q L Server Management Studio using the Export Data-tier Application wizard or sqlpackage. exe with an export action. Azure Database Migration Service is a managed service that enables online and offline migrations from on-premises S Q L Server to Azure targets. For online migrations, DMS performs an initial full data load and then continuously applies incremental changes so the target stays synchronized until you choose to cut over. The practical benefit is that your application can continue operating on the source during the bulk of migration and only needs a short maintenance window for cutover. Provisioning DMS and executing a safe cutover requires a sequence of deliberate steps. First, provision a DMS instance in the Azure portal in the same region and subscription as your target where possible. Next, create a migration project and specify the source type (S Q L Server) and the Azure target (S Q L Database or Managed Instance). Configure endpoints by providing connection strings and credentials for both source and target; validate these endpoints to confirm connectivity. Select the databases and tables to migrate and choose online migration to enable continuous synchronization. Start the migration: DMS performs the initial full load, then applies changes incrementally. Monitor the migration project until the change backlog is minimal and run validation tests against the target to ensure data fidelity. A common mistake is performing cutover without exercising validation tests; always perform the cutover in a test window and have a rollback plan ready.
